title: Supervision 5 short answers
description: 4 short-answer questions on this week’s lectures, all of them handed in.
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 5. There are four short-answer questions, on gases in the blood, the control of breathing at altitude, and lung function tests. Answer all four, then hand them in together.

  • Marks. Each question is marked out of 5. Answer in bullet points, and aim for at least 5 separate, precise points: a number, a mechanism or a piece of evidence is worth more than a general statement.
  • Calculations. The calculator is at the top of the page. Show your working, and give units.
  • Equations. Type simple ones into your text, as you’d write them by hand (× is among the special characters, under Ω). For one with a fraction, use the formula tool, Σ. Say what each equation means, and then use it.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your work.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your work, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Saving. Your work is saved in this browser as you type, so you can stop and come back to it. It stays here until you submit it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your work and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: Content and saturation
questions.text:
Distinguish between the oxygen content and the oxygen saturation of arterial blood. Why is carbon monoxide poisoning more dangerous than an anaemia that halves the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood?

Answer in bullet points.
questions.guidance:
Points a good answer makes. Each is worth about a mark.

  • Saturation: the percentage of haemoglobin’s O2-binding sites that are occupied, set by the PO2 (about 97.5% at 100 mmHg, 75% at 40 mmHg).
  • Content: the volume of O2 per litre of blood: 1.39 mL per gram of haemoglobin × the haemoglobin concentration × saturation, plus the dissolved O2 (0.03 mL/L per mmHg: only 3 mL/L at 100 mmHg). About 200 mL/L normally. Content, not PO2 or saturation, is what delivers O2.
  • Anaemia: saturation and PO2 are normal, the content is low; the curve keeps its shape, so the blood still unloads at the tissues’ PO2 (about 25 mL/L between 100 and 40 mmHg, against about 49 normally).
  • Carbon monoxide binds about 200 times more tightly than O2, occupying sites, and shifts the curve of the remaining haemoglobin to the left, so it gives up little O2 at the tissues’ PO2 (about 8 mL/L).
  • And it’s hidden: arterial PO2 and PCO2 are normal, so there is no drive to breathe harder; the patient looks pink; a pulse oximeter reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin and gives a normal saturation.

questions.title: Carrying CO₂
questions.text:
Describe how carbon dioxide is carried in the blood, and explain the Haldane effect.

Answer in bullet points.
questions.guidance:
Points a good answer makes. Each is worth about a mark.

  • As bicarbonate (about 70%): CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ HCO3− + H+, slow in plasma, fast in red cells with carbonic anhydrase; HCO3− leaves the cell in exchange for Cl− (the chloride shift); the H+ is buffered by haemoglobin.
  • Dissolved (5–10%): CO2 is about 20 times more soluble than O2, so dissolved CO2 is a real part of transport (about 32 mL per litre of plasma at 46 mmHg).
  • As carbamino compounds (about 20%), mostly carbaminohaemoglobin, bound to amine groups.
  • The Haldane effect: deoxygenated blood carries more CO2 at the same PCO2, because deoxyhaemoglobin is a weaker acid (a better buffer of H+, pulling the reaction towards bicarbonate) and forms carbamino compounds more readily.
  • Its importance: in the tissues, as O2 is unloaded, more CO2 is loaded; in the lungs, oxygenation drives CO2 off. It accounts for a large part of the CO2 exchanged, with only a small difference in PCO2 (40 against 46 mmHg). It’s the counterpart of the Bohr effect.

questions.title: Breathing at altitude
questions.text:
Explain how ventilation changes over the first few days after arrival at high altitude, and why.

Answer in bullet points.
questions.guidance:
Points a good answer makes. Each is worth about a mark.

  • The stimulus: the fraction of O2 stays at 21%, but the barometric pressure is lower, so the inspired and arterial PO2 fall; below about 60 mmHg, the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) drive ventilation up.
  • The brake: the extra ventilation lowers PaCO2, causing a respiratory alkalosis; the central chemoreceptors sense the rise in pH of the CSF and reduce the drive, so the first rise in ventilation is blunted.
  • Over days: the kidneys excrete HCO3− (metabolic compensation), and the HCO3− of the CSF falls too, bringing the pH of blood and CSF back towards normal. That removes the brake, so ventilation rises further: ventilatory acclimatisation.
  • Use the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2)); a lower PCO2 raises pH until [HCO3−] falls in proportion.
  • Other adjustments: more 2,3-BPG (a right shift, helping unloading), then more erythropoietin and red cells; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, with the risk of high-altitude pulmonary oedema.

questions.title: Two spirometry results
questions.text:
Patient X has an FEV1 of 1.3 L and an FVC of 3.4 L. Patient Y has an FEV1 of 2.0 L and an FVC of 2.3 L. Both have a low diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide. Interpret each result, and explain how each pattern arises.

Answer in bullet points.
questions.guidance:
Points a good answer makes. Each is worth about a mark.

  • X: FEV1/FVC = 1.3 / 3.4 = 0.38, below 0.7: an obstructive pattern. The air leaves slowly.
  • Its mechanism, with the low diffusing capacity: emphysema (COPD). Lost elastic recoil and lost tethering of the small airways move the equal pressure point into them, so they collapse early in a forced expiration (effort-independent flow, air trapping, a high TLC); destroyed alveolar walls reduce the area for diffusion.
  • Y: FEV1/FVC = 2.0 / 2.3 = 0.87, normal or high, with a small FVC: a restrictive pattern (a low TLC would confirm it).
  • Its mechanism, with the low diffusing capacity: pulmonary fibrosis. Stiff, less compliant lungs have small volumes, but their strong recoil and open airways empty them fast; the thickened interstitium lengthens the path for diffusion (Fick’s law).
  • For more marks: why carbon monoxide is used to measure diffusing capacity (it binds haemoglobin so tightly that its uptake is limited by diffusion, not by blood flow); in asthma the diffusing capacity is usually normal, and the obstruction reverses with a bronchodilator.
